lesson.text: Quick memory: in a landscape, how do things far away look? (Smaller, paler and bluer.) Today: a drawing trick that makes a road or a room go deep into the distance.
Stand on a long straight road: its two edges seem to meet far away, though they never really do. Artists call the point where they seem to meet the vanishing point.
The vanishing point sits on the horizon line, and the horizon line is always at your eye level. Climb a hill and the horizon rises with your eyes; lie on the grass and it drops.
In one-point perspective, every line that goes away from you (artists call them orthogonals) is drawn to the one vanishing point. Lines across stay flat, and upright lines stay upright.
Worked example: to draw a road, draw the horizon and put a dot on it. Then draw lines from the bottom corners of the page to the dot. Posts beside the road get smaller the nearer they are to the dot.
A room works the same way: draw the back wall as a small rectangle round the vanishing point, then join its corners to the corners of the page. The floor, ceiling and walls appear.

Around 1415, the architect Filippo Brunelleschi showed how perspective works, in Florence, Italy. In 1435 Leon Battista Alberti wrote down its rules. Raphael's The School of Athens (1511) is a famous example.
Try it in the world: stand at the end of a long straight path or a row of fences in your world and look along it. Where do its edges seem to meet? Next: Greek and Roman art.

exercises.prompt: What is the marked point called?
exercises.hint: It is where the road's edges seem to meet.
exercises.explain: The road's edges meet at the vanishing point.

exercises.prompt: In one-point perspective, lines that go away from you all meet at one point.
exercises.hint: Think of the road's two edges.
exercises.explain: True: they all meet at the vanishing point, on the horizon.

exercises.hint: What happens to the horizon when you climb a hill?
choices: always at the top of the page
always at the bottom of the page
exercises.explain: The horizon line is always at your eye level, so it moves up and down with your eyes.

exercises.prompt: Match each word to its meaning.
exercises.explain: The vanishing point is where lines meet, the horizon is at eye level, orthogonals go to the point, and the foreground is nearest you.

exercises.prompt: Posts stand beside a road. What happens to them as they get nearer the vanishing point?
exercises.explain: Further away means smaller, so the posts shrink towards the vanishing point.

exercises.prompt: Put the steps for drawing a road in one-point perspective in order.
exercises.hint: You need the horizon before you can put a point on it.
items: Add posts that shrink towards the point
Draw lines from the bottom corners to the point
Put a vanishing point on it
exercises.explain: Horizon, vanishing point, the road's edges to the point, then posts that shrink towards it.

exercises.prompt: The upright sides of a door facing you stay upright in one-point perspective.
exercises.hint: Only the lines going away from you go to the point.
exercises.explain: True: upright lines stay upright and lines across stay flat; only lines going away meet at the point.

exercises.hint: It goes right across the picture, where the land meets the sky.
exercises.explain: The marked line is the horizon line, at the viewer's eye level.

exercises.prompt: In a room drawing, does each line go to the vanishing point, or stay flat or upright?
items: where a wall meets the ceiling
the top edge of the back wall
the side of the back door
exercises.hint: Does the line go away from you, or does it face you?
exercises.explain: Lines going away from you, along the floor and the walls, go to the point. The back wall and its door face you, so their lines stay flat or upright.

exercises.prompt: You look down from a high tower. Where is the horizon line in your drawing?
exercises.hint: The horizon is always at your eye level. Where are your eyes now?
choices: high on the page, at your eye level
at the very bottom of the page
it is not there at all
exercises.explain: Your eyes are high up, so the horizon is high on the page and you see lots of ground below it.

exercises.prompt: Who showed how perspective works, around 1415 in Florence?
exercises.hint: He was an architect in Florence, Italy.
exercises.explain: Filippo Brunelleschi, an architect, showed how perspective works around 1415 in Florence.

exercises.prompt: Five posts stand in a row. On the page the first is 16 cm tall and each next one is half as tall. How tall is the 4th post, in cm?
exercises.hint: Halve the height again for each post along the row.
exercises.explain: 16, then 8, 4 and 2: the 4th post is 2 cm tall.

exercises.prompt: A road's two edges really do meet far away.
exercises.hint: Walk along the road: do the edges ever touch?
exercises.explain: False: they only seem to meet. The road stays the same width; it just looks narrower further away.

exercises.prompt: Where do the lines from the four corners of this room go?
exercises.hint: Follow the dashed lines from the corners.
choices: to the corners of the door
to the bottom of the page
exercises.explain: All four go to the vanishing point in the middle of the back wall.

exercises.prompt: In a drawing of a straight road, sort the lines: to the vanishing point, or flat or upright?
items: the top of a fence going away
a railway sleeper across the track
exercises.hint: Only lines that go away from you meet at the vanishing point.
exercises.explain: To the point: the road's edges, the fence top and the rails all go away from you. Flat or upright: posts stand upright, and a sleeper lies across, facing you.
